claims.text: The initial as-cast refractory HEA is homogeneous, single-phase, and BCC.
A post-cast heat treatment or aging process can induce controlled precipitation of nanoscale secondary phases in the refractory HEA.
The induced precipitates have a size and spatial distribution that allow them to act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Nanoscale secondary-phase precipitates impede dislocation glide.
The precipitates interact with thermoelastic strain fields.
Precipitate-induced restriction of dislocation motion improves high-temperature yield strength.
Precipitates alter internal friction or damping behavior under cyclic thermal loads.
Relative to the untreated homogeneous alloy, the precipitate-containing heat-treated alloy will have higher high-temperature yield strength.
Relative to the untreated homogeneous alloy, the precipitate-containing heat-treated alloy will show a measurable change in its high-temperature thermoelastic damping profile.
Restricted dislocation mobility may reduce damping in the precipitate-containing alloy.
The proposed behavior applies between approximately 800°C and 1200°C under controlled atmosphere and mechanical loading.
The proposed mechanism requires the precipitate phase to remain stable and well distributed under the high-temperature test conditions.
The proposed mechanism requires an alloy composition capable of forming a coherent precipitate–matrix structure.
Complex precipitation kinetics and interactions among multiple principal elements make the magnitude of the property changes uncertain.
